newsitem.title: LEBANON: Hizbollah eyes comeback from south Lebanon polls.
newsitem.headline: Hizbollah eyes comeback from south Lebanon polls.

text.p: The fourth stage of Lebanon's month-long general elections ended peacefully in the Shi'ite heartland in the south where the militant Hizbollah hopes to score a win to reverse harsh defeats in earlier rounds.
The Interior ministry said 48 percent of south Lebanon's 552,000 voters cast ballots to choose 23 deputies in the 10-hour polls on Sunday, compared with 38 percent in 1992.
Sunday's turnout was the highest so far in the polls in which Beirut, north Lebanon and Mount Lebanon voted on the three previous Sundays with 31, 40 and 45 percent respective turnout.

The eastern Bekaa valley votes next Sunday, ending the month-long polls. That vote, coupled with the south Lebanon polls, will decide the distribution of the majority of seats set for Lebanon's 1.3 million Shi'ites in the 128-seat parliament.
They also determine the popularity of the pro-Iranian Hizbollah (Party of God) which seeks to win four deputies from south Lebanon and three MPs and two allies from the Bekaa.
The dusty impoverished Shi'ite villages of both areas are traditional recruiting grounds for the guerrilla group fighting to oust Israeli forces from a south Lebanon border zone.

The fundamentalist group, two of whose candidates lost their parliamentary seats in earlier rounds, fielded candidates in the remaining two voting rounds under a Syrian-brokered pact with its rival Shi'ite group, the secular movement Amal.

Fears of violence at the ballot box were allayed after Syria, Beirut's main power, forged the eleventh hour deal to run a joint Amal-Hizbollah list of candidates in the south despite political enmity and an 1987-90 war between the two factions.

Hizbollah had eight MPs and four allies in the outgoing assembly but appears unlikely to match that number in the current election. If all its candidates win, its representation in the new house will be cut by one MP and two supporters.

Some 8,000 heavily-armed troops, backed by armoured carriers, ensured security as voters, including bearded men and women in Islamic chadours, voted in segregated booths to choose representatives to the half-Christian, half-Moslem parliament.

Running against the Amal-Hizbollah alliance, headed by Amal chief and parliament speaker Nabih Berri, were a 10-member leftist ticket and a 15-member list headed by Kamel Assad, scion of a feudal Shi'ite family and former parliament speaker.
Vote counting began after polls closed at 5.00 p.m. (1400 GMT) without incident and results are expected on Monday.
Hizbollah followers in cars waved yellow flags showing a fist holding an AK-47 assault rifle while Amal men waved green flags, as voting proceeded briskly in the cities of Sidon and Tyre.

There was an election battle for two Sunni Moslem seats for Sidon not included on the joint 21-member ticket. Amal backers voted for Bahia Hariri, sister of Prime Minister Rafik al-Hariri, and an ally, while Hizbollah, a Hariri foe, urged followers to vote for two other candidates.
A private watchdog group, the Lebanese Association for the Democracy of Elections (LADE), reported a drop in abuses during Sunday's vote compared to the three earlier rounds of voting.

But violations cited by LADE on Sunday included fraudulent voting in the name of dead people or emigrantsd in Burghuliyyeh and Tyre, and police illegally entering many polling stations, some of which lacked isolating curtains for voting in secret.
It said security forces pressured voters to vote for certain candidates in Bint Jbeil and noted the absence of names from voter lists in some areas, a recurrent problem in the polls.
